The proposed pilot

Start small.
Measure what matters.

Can a community kiosk help people facing access barriers complete an appropriate clinical assessment? We propose a supervised study to find out.

Proposal · Seeking clinical and community partners

A focused first study

Two settings. One complete pathway.

2proposed community sites

One urban venue and one rural hub, selected with local communities.

160adults in the main study

Approximately 80 in the kiosk pathway and 80 in an existing supported route.

22indicative programme weeks

Including preparation, eight weeks of main recruitment, follow-up and evaluation.

All figures are proposed planning assumptions. Sites, funding, partners and authorisations are not confirmed. Required reviews or readiness work may extend the schedule.

What we would test

A more accessible first interaction. A real route into care.

The first version would offer a bounded symptom questionnaire, optional voice input, supported languages and a patient-confirmed history. A clinician would review recommendations before they reach the participant.

The receiving care service would agree referral capacity and follow-up responsibilities before recruitment starts. A completed kiosk session would not count as a completed referral.

One visit, end to end

  1. A facilitator explains the service, information use and optional research.
  2. The participant uses their allocated intake route and checks the recorded history.
  3. A clinician determines the appropriate next action.
  4. A navigator helps arrange the next contact and checks understanding.
  5. The team records whether the assessment was completed within the agreed timeframe.

Rollout

Earn the next step.

Each stage depends on the preceding work being ready, with clinical oversight throughout.

Weeks 1–4 · Or longer if needed

Agree the foundations

Confirm venues, clinical scope, evaluation design, care capacity, governance and data responsibilities. Determine the applicable review and authorisation routes.

Weeks 5–8

Design with communities. Rehearse with clinicians.

Run community discussions and fictional-case usability sessions. Test urgent scenarios, language errors, accessibility, record retrieval and fallback arrangements.

Weeks 9–16 · After readiness clearance

Launch one site, then two

Begin with about 20 separate soft-launch participants at the first site. Once problems are resolved, run the 160-person comparative study across both sites with weekly monitoring.

Weeks 17–20

Close the follow-up loop

Finish outcome collection and interviews. Record unknown outcomes explicitly and hand over any continuing clinical follow-up.

Weeks 21–22

Evaluate before expanding

Review feasibility, comparative outcomes, incidents, language differences and costs. Decide together whether to revise, extend or propose a larger study.

Community design, usability and soft-launch participants are additional to the 160-person main sample. The timetable is indicative; recruitment does not begin before the relevant requirements are met.

Meaningful evidence

Measure access, safety and understanding.

01 · Completed care

Did people reach assessment?

Track appropriate follow-up assessments within a clinician-defined deadline, capped at 14 days for the primary analysis. Report those with no follow-up indicated separately.

02 · Safe guidance

Were urgent concerns handled appropriately?

Measure missed urgent concerns, clinician overrides, material language errors and near misses. Compare AI urgency output only after a clinician records an independent judgement.

03 · Accessible use

Could people understand and complete the journey?

Review completion, help needed, next-step comprehension and outcomes by language and relevant audience group. Include community feedback on trust.

04 · Practical delivery

Would the pathway work for a provider?

Measure history usefulness, correction effort, staff time and full costs. Compare with an existing supported intake route using equivalent access to care and interpretation.

This feasibility sample will produce uncertain estimates, particularly within language groups. It will not establish mortality benefit or validate autonomous triage. Zero observed serious events would not prove safety.

A shared undertaking

Build the service around the community.

We are seeking a healthcare delivery partner, community venues, representatives of the intended users, an evaluation partner and language expertise. A potential innovation partner could support funding, evaluation and introductions across this network.

Our proposal is relevant to AstraZeneca’s published priorities in health equity and collaborative innovation. It is not an existing AstraZeneca partnership or service.

Responsibilities before launch

  • Clinical partner: care pathways, review, referral capacity and incident response.
  • Community partners: trusted recruitment, accessible venues and co-design.
  • Evaluator: protocol, appropriate reviews, outcome definitions and analysis.
  • Product team: reliable software, secure access, version control and support.

Clinical and information governance

Define the safeguards before enrolment.

The sponsor and healthcare partner would determine the applicable research and medical-device requirements, data roles, processing arrangements and reviews. Supervision does not automatically exempt a prototype from those requirements.

Participation in research would be optional, with a human route into care. The pilot would use a provider-approved record system and authorised access. We would not place identifiable clinical information on a blockchain.

Not a fixed price or secured funding. Excludes major new product development, regulatory submission fees, any additional required insurance, and downstream clinical investigations or treatment. Local quotes and partner commitments are needed.

The Finnish context

A pilot grounded in national priorities.

Finland’s strategy highlights health literacy, multilingual communication and trust, while noting that timely access to care must also work. Its roadmap includes accessible digital symptom assessment integrated with existing services.
